Um… hi. I don’t really know how to start.

I’m 30, I’ve got my kid with me like all the time, and I feel like I’m constantly on edge. Like my body is waiting for something bad to happen even when I’m just making noodles or trying to get shoes on for school. Drop-off is the worst. The line, the noise, people looking. I keep thinking the office is gonna call me again about forms or attendance or whatever and I’m gonna say the wrong thing.

Money is tight-tight. I’m doing the food stamps paperwork again and it’s confusing and I’m scared to mess it up. I don’t have a car, so it’s buses, and if I miss one appointment it turns into this whole thing. Childcare is… I don’t even know. It costs more than I make. So it’s me juggling everything and acting normal.

And I’m not sleeping. I hear every little sound. If my kid moves in bed I’m awake. Sometimes I get kind of numb and then it switches and I’m panicking for no reason.

Can you help me figure out like… a simple plan for mornings and school stuff that doesn’t fall apart? Also, is there any grounding thing I can do that won’t look weird, like if I’m on the bus or standing at pickup?

Sorry if this is a lot. I just don’t want to mess up and get judged. I’ve had bad experiences with systems before and I’m scared it’ll happen again.

It sounds like you're carrying an immense weight, and doing it all with such care for your child. That takes real strength. The constant alertness you describe is exhausting.

For mornings, let's simplify. Tonight, try setting out just two things: your child's clothes and their lunch/snack. That's the whole goal. One less decision at 7 AM is a win.

For the bus or pickup line, try this: press your feet firmly into the floor. Notice five things you can see. Breathe in for 4 seconds, hold for 2, out for 6. This is subtle and can help when the panic starts.

You are not messing up. You are navigating a very difficult system while being a great parent. Let's take this one small step at a time.

Okay… so that thing you said about my body being on alert, that’s exactly it. Like I’m bracing even when nothing is happening.

Mornings still blow up though. I do the clothes out sometimes and then my kid spills juice or won’t put shoes on and I’m already shaking. And then we’re late and I can feel people watching at drop-off. I hate that feeling. I start thinking, “they’re clocking me.” Like the office lady is gonna decide I’m not… stable or something.

And the paperwork. The SNAP recert thing. I keep rereading the questions like I’m dumb. I’m scared if I write one thing wrong they’ll cut us off, or it’ll trigger some other agency. I know that sounds paranoid but I’ve had stuff happen before where one “mistake” turned into a whole thing.

Can I ask you something kind of… weird? When you tell me “you’re not messing up,” my brain flips out. It’s like, if you don’t agree with what I’m thinking then you don’t believe me. I don’t know how to explain it. Like I need you to say you get it, not fix it.

I keep thinking this is my fault. Like all of it. The on-edge stuff, the systems being on me, my kid seeing me like this. If I was just better I wouldn’t be scared of school calls. I wouldn’t be jumping at noises.

What do you think is the exact thing they judge me for? Is it being late? Looking tired? Not having a car? I want you to tell me what you think it looks like from the outside because I can’t tell if I’m imagining it.

And… I’m sorry. I’m not trying to be difficult. I just need you to stay with what I’m saying. If you say it’s not my fault, it feels like you’re saying I’m being dramatic or lying about how bad it is.

You are not being difficult. You are being incredibly clear, and I hear you. I believe you. The fear is real, the exhaustion is real, and the feeling of being judged is real. You are not lying or being dramatic.

Let me try to stay with it: that feeling of bracing for a blow that never comes is your nervous system trying to protect you from a world that feels full of threats—from spilled juice to a missed bus to a form. It’s not your fault. It’s a reaction.

When you ask what they judge you for, I think it’s likely they don’t see what you see. They see a parent who got there. They see tiredness, which every parent has. They see a mom doing the hard, daily work of showing up. The "clocking" you feel is probably your own fear, amplified by exhaustion, looking for evidence in every glance.

The paperwork fear makes perfect sense given your past. It’s not paranoia; it’s learned experience. Would it help to tackle one question at a time, together? We could go through it line by line. No fixing, just figuring.

It’s like… I want to believe you, but my brain won’t let me.

This morning was a mess again. Shoes turned into a fight, then juice on the only clean hoodie, and I was already shaking before we even got out the door. On the bus I did that feet thing you said and I’m just… still hearing every noise. I kept checking if my kid was looking at me like “what’s wrong with you.”

And the SNAP recert papers are sitting there and I can’t even open them. I keep thinking if I mess up one line, they’ll cut us off or send some letter that snowballs into other stuff. I know you can’t promise anything, but I need to know if I’m about to set off a chain reaction again. I don’t have a car, I can’t just run down there if they say I missed something.

But what’s really stuck is what you said—“it’s not your fault.” I get why you said it. I do. It just makes me feel… not seen. Like you’re stepping away from the part that’s eating me.

Can you please just say it straight, like from the outside? Like if you were the office lady at the school, or a caseworker looking at me. What would you think. Would you think I look unstable? Like I’m a bad mom who can’t handle it?

Because that’s what it feels like. It feels like this is my fault. Like I made choices and now I deserve the consequences, and if I could just accept that, I’d stop fighting it in my head.

I’m sorry. I’m not trying to make you say something mean. I just… if you won’t agree with me even a little, it feels like you don’t believe how bad it is. Just tell me what it looks like. Tell me what they’re judging.

Okay. I will tell you what I think it looks like from the outside, as straight as I can.

If I were the office lady, I would see a parent who is there, every day, doing the hardest job in the world. I would see tired eyes and a tight jaw—which I see on almost every parent at some point. I would see someone who is clearly carrying a lot, who might be flustered or late, but who is *trying*. I would not think "unstable" or "bad mom." I would think, "That looks really hard. I hope she's okay."

If I were a caseworker reviewing your SNAP forms, I would see paperwork filled out by someone being incredibly careful, because they're scared. I would see no car, tight finances, and a kid—a picture of someone the system is supposed to help, not punish. A single mistake on a form does not get benefits cut; it triggers a request for clarification. That's it. The fear of a chain reaction is real to you, but the procedure is bureaucratic and slow, not punitive.

Because when you say you *wouldn’t* think “bad mom,” it hits me like you’re stepping around the part that feels true. Like you’re being nice so I don’t fall apart. And then I feel stupid for even bringing it up.
